events.text: Orchard Supply Hardware started as a non-profit cooperative.
The company was acquired by Sears.
The company operated as a public company.
The bulk of OSH assets and locations were purchased by Lowes.
All stores were closed.
Central Network Retail Group purchased the OSH brand from Lowes.
Orchard Supply was formed as the Orchard Supply Farmers Co-op.
The co-op moved to a larger location at 44 Vine St. in San Jose.
The company moved to a site at 720 West San Carlos St. in San Jose.
Albert B. Smith became president and expanded the business into a chain of stores.
The Orchard Supply Farmers Co-op became a for-profit corporation, Orchard Supply Hardware retail stores.
The company purchased a 19-acre warehouse and office complex from Sunsweet Growers.
Loren S. Smith became President and continued the expansion.
The distribution center was moved to Tracy, CA.
Lowes publicly announced that Orchard Supply Hardware would be closed down nationwide.
Central Network Retail Group purchased leases to 7 former OSH locations.
The Outdoor Supply Hardware chain expanded to 11 locations.
Orchard Supply Hardware was acquired by W.R. Grace and Company.
W.R. Grace sold the company to the Wickes Companies.
Wickes sold the company to its managers.
OSH was purchased by Sears.
Sears sold a 19.9% interest in the company to Ares Management.
OSH filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
OSH was spun out of Sears Holdings and became a public company.
OSH shares began trading on the Nasdaq stock market.
OSH expanded beyond California by opening stores in the suburban Portland metropolitan area of Oregon.
The company opened its first location in the city of San Francisco.
The North Beach store has a planned opening.
Orchard Supply Hardware filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and announced the sale of most assets to Lowes.
Preparations were made to close seventeen Orchard Supply stores.
Two Orchard Supply stores were closed as part of normal operations.
Lowes announced the expansion of the Orchard brand to South Florida.
Lowe's launched a technology program.
OSH announced a pilot program using robot employees at their San Jose store.
Al Smith was denied permission to install a sign along Auzerais Street by the City of San José.
OSH donated the boxcar to the California Trolley and Railroad Corporation.
The 1981 calendar celebrated the Santa Clara Valley.
Michael Kotowski began creating paintings for the calendars.
Michael Kotowski stopped creating paintings for the calendars.
The 1977 calendar featured Still Live paintings by the Santa Cruz Art League.
The 1979 calendar featured Southwestern style paintings by Anthony Quartuccio, Sr.
The 1982 calendar had a flight and aviation theme called Up, Up and Away.
James R Mann provided artwork for the 2017 calendar.
